content: Since the introduction of ready-to-use therapeutic food (RUTF) in the 1990s, studies have shown that most children with severe acute malnutrition (SAM) can be treated safely without requiring hospitalization, provided they have no medical complications, are eating well, and are gaining weight. In 2007, a joint statement by the United Nations endorsed outpatient care for children aged 6–59 months with SAM who present with no medical complications and have a good appetite. This statement also recommended the use of mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) measurements as an independent criterion for screening children for SAM. The transition from the NCHS growth reference to the WHO growth standards in 2006 led to a revision of the cut-off values for indicators of SAM. In 2009, a joint United Nations statement endorsed a MUAC of less than 115 mm as a diagnostic criterion for SAM in children, given its high predictive value for mortality. MUAC is measured using simple arm bands marked in millimeter graduations, which can be color-coded for ease of use. These bands can be used and interpreted by healthcare workers with appropriate training. The use of a single MUAC cut-off value for identifying SAM in children aged 6–59 months was noted to have programmatic advantages. However, MUAC and weight-for-height indicators do not always correlate when identifying children with SAM. Approximately 40% of children classified as having SAM by one indicator are similarly classified by the other. The agreement between these criteria varies significantly across different settings and geographic locations. Community studies comparing sensitivity-specificity curves (receiver operating characteristic curves) have shown that MUAC is better at identifying children at high risk of death. The 1999 recommendations for hospital discharge included criteria such as achieving a weight-for-height Z-score of ≥ -1 or ≥ 90% of the median NCHS/WHO reference values. In 2009, a joint United Nations statement proposed a single discharge criterion of 15% (or 20%, depending on the local context) weight gain over the oedema-free weight at enrollment, along with the absence of oedema for two weeks. Data from outpatient care programs in Malawi and Ethiopia suggested that a 15% weight gain would result in 50% of children with SAM meeting or exceeding 80% of the median weight-for-height of the NCHS reference. However, concerns were raised about the validity of this criterion as an indicator of nutritional recovery. In many settings, only the MUAC cut-off value of ≥ 125 mm was applied for discharge. The discharge cut-off value of MUAC ≥ 125 mm was based on historical cohort studies from Bangladesh, Malawi, and Uganda, which suggested that the mortality risk at this cut-off did not exceed 1/10,000 per day. However, the safety of using changes in MUAC as an indicator of recovery progress during nutritional rehabilitation, and a single cut-off value to indicate recovery, has not been validated. The WHO, with support from the guideline development group, aimed to provide guidance on admission and discharge criteria for children aged 6–59 months with SAM. This included admission cut-off values for screening indicators, discharge cut-off values for different admission indicators, criteria for inpatient and outpatient care, and the transition from inpatient to outpatient care after stabilization. A systematic review was conducted to examine admission and discharge criteria for SAM in children aged 6–59 months. Eleven relevant epidemiological studies were identified, though three used admission cut-off values that did not correspond to the WHO definition of SAM. Most studies were conducted in African countries, with five taking place in the same setting in Malawi, where a high proportion of children had oedema. The majority of studies involved uncomplicated cases of SAM managed in outpatient programs. Five studies used MUAC as an inclusion criterion, while the other seven used weight-for-height for enrollment but reported on MUAC gain during nutritional rehabilitation. Both low weight-for-height and low MUAC identify children at increased risk of mortality, but the children identified by each indicator may differ. In one study involving 34,937 children from multiple countries, the MUAC < 115 mm criterion failed to detect SAM in up to 75% of children identified as having SAM by weight-for-height < -3 Z-score using the WHO growth standards. No randomized studies were identified comparing outcomes of nutritional rehabilitation in children admitted based on MUAC versus weight-for-height Z-scores. Only one study compared mortality risk in hospitalized children based on these two indicators. Children with MUAC ≤ 115 mm were more likely to present with signs of oedematous malnutrition, stunting, and subcostal indrawing, and were more frequently younger and female compared to those admitted with weight-for-height ≤ -3 Z-score. The guideline group noted that the development of RUTF has made outpatient management of SAM more feasible and safer. Active community screening allows for early identification and treatment of SAM as outpatients, avoiding the risks and challenges of inpatient care, such as nosocomial infections, transportation issues, and family disruptions. MUAC has facilitated community screening due to its simplicity and ease of use. The group also discussed the implications of using WHO growth standards, which are likely to identify a larger population with SAM compared to NCHS growth reference values. This has significant implications for countries in South and Southeast Asia, where many infants and young children would be classified as having SAM using the WHO standards. While both weight-for-height and MUAC are effective methods for assessing wasting, they require training and methodical implementation to ensure reliable assessments. Even after training, significant variation has been observed in healthcare workers' measurements and classifications. The guideline group emphasized that children identified using weight-for-height do not consistently have MUAC < 115 mm, and vice versa. The evidence suggests that the two indicators do not always identify the same populations. There is limited evidence on the most appropriate MUAC cut-off value to indicate nutritional recovery. The 2006 WHO growth standards suggest that a MUAC of 125 mm corresponds to a MUAC-for-age Z-score < -3 for older children, particularly males. Using this single cut-off value may result in children with SAM being discharged prematurely, especially older male children. Adopting a higher MUAC cut-off value could address this issue but would result in longer treatment durations. Using MUAC-for-age or MUAC-for-height Z-scores ≥ -2 would allow for the discharge of children who are no longer malnourished and avoid inappropriate treatment of younger children. The guideline group acknowledged that simple and uniform cut-off values are programmatically helpful, but the evidence suggests that the sensitivity and specificity of MUAC measurements compared to weight-for-height differ significantly across age, height, and sex.
